transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~75 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood), Maya Chen (Aurora Platform Eng), Liam O'Neill (Aurora SRE), Priya Kapoor (Aurora Security), Diego Ruiz (Aurora ML)

Summary:
Quick network diagnostics + KV-cache and batching workshop to isolate tail-latency spikes seen in Aurora's private VPC deployment. Focus areas: PrivateLink topology, NAT hairpinning, MTU mismatches, DNS resolution and cache warming, KV cache eviction patterns, batch sizing for mixed seq lengths, and minimal quantization tradeoffs for 16->8-bit.

Topics:
- PrivateLink / cross-account privatelink routing quirks
- Egress NAT vs. egress-only subnets and hairpin tests
- DNS TTLs and conditional forwarding to resolver endpoints
- MTU and fragmentation observed across on-prem VPN tunnel
- KV cache TTL/eviction and warmup behavior with varied prompt prefixes
- Continuous batching vs. fixed-window batching for mixed short/long sequences
- Quantization: int8 perf gains vs. slight perplexity regressions

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. we're gonna kick off, we got about an hour fifteen. Samir is gonna drive the tech bits. quick intro round?
[00:08] Maya Chen: Hi I'm Maya, platform at Aurora, looking to get these p99 spikes under control.
[00:11] Liam O'Neill: Liam here SRE, we see tail spikes primarily during batch cold starts after cache evictions.
[00:16] Samir Patel: Cool, thanks. Before we dig in, can you share the top-line of your topology? private VPC with cross-account privatelink into our infra, right?
[00:25] Diego Ruiz: Correct. We have a privatelink endpoint in our prod account pointing to Redwood's service endpoint in your account. There is an on-prem VPN to the prod VPC as well.
[00:33] Jordan Lee: Noted — sometimes the VPN MTU leads to fragmentation which increases packetization overhead for KV cache RPCs.
[00:40] Priya Kapoor: quick pause — from security, we need to ensure we don't route egress over the public internet; we want all egress to go through our egress NAT with inspection.
[00:47] Alex Kim: Got it. Two constraints: PrivateLink for control plane and model endpoint traffic, and egress through your NAT for outbound only. We'll keep that in mind.

[00:55] Samir Patel: Okay let's replay the p99 scenario: what we've seen in other customers is a stack of factors — small MTU causing fragmentation of KV cache RPCs, DNS resolving to an older resolver and then hitting the longer path, and hairpin NAT on privatelink when callers are in same VPC but IP mapping forces double-hop. any of that ring a bell?
[01:12] Liam O'Neill: hairpin was actually our suspicion. we saw an increase in packets/time when the caller was in a private subnet that had a route through the NAT gateway to reach the privatelink, instead of staying local.
[01:22] Samir Patel: that explains the extra ~40-60ms. If packets hairpin through NAT you get conn-track overhead and sometimes PATH MTU discovery interactions.
[01:29] Maya Chen: we do have an egress-only internet gateway for some flows — maybe that is mis-configured.

[01:35] Samir Patel: Let's bring up the KV cache specifics. Diego, when the model cold-starts, what eviction policy are you using and what's your typical prompt prefix length distribution?
[01:43] Diego Ruiz: LRU with a 30-minute TTL. Prompt prefixes vary a lot — 60% short (<=50 tokens), 30% medium (50-300 tokens), 10% long (>300).
[01:52] Samir Patel: Mixed seqs are tricky. Continuous batching helps for short ones, but long ones block the queue for tokens if you don't shard. Are you using request partitioning by estimated output length?
[02:01] Diego Ruiz: no, not yet. we're just feeding requests as they come.
[02:04] Samir Patel: That will amplify p99. Best practice: apply mixed-batch scheduling — hold a tiny window for short requests (50ms) and trigger immediate flush for longer ones, or use estimated token budgets to route to dedicated long-seq workers.

[02:12] [02:15] (background: someone typing)
[02:18] Liam O'Neill: question — how does KV cache RPC size vary? are we talking multiple MBs per call?
[02:23] Samir Patel: Typically, a KV cache lookup for cached prefixes is small — a few KBs. The big cost is when you're sending large KV updates during caching warmups or sending full attention KV snapshots for longer histories. Those can be hundreds of KBs, and if MTU is low and the link fragments them, you pay extra latency.
[02:40] Alex Kim: Also note that some on-prem VPNs have low TCP window sizes which can interact poorly with many small RPCs; worth checking iperf tests.

[02:47] Diego Ruiz: we did a quick iperf last week — throughput looks fine but MTU showed 1400 on the tunnel, while our instances are 9001 internally.
[02:55] Samir Patel: there's your culprit. When jumbo frames are expected but the tunnel is 1400, you get fragmentation. For KV cache interactions that are many small packets, that's worse than a few large ones because of packet reassembly and head-of-line blocking.

[03:05] Priya Kapoor: From security we prefer not to change our tunnel MTU on the on-prem side without change approval process. What mitigations can we do instead?
[03:12] Samir Patel: two options: 1) reduce per-RPC payload by compressing KV payloads (we can enable gzip for cache transfers) and chunking more aggressively; 2) move heavy cache warmups over an internal data channel that respects the small MTU — like a staged warmup via S3 or a direct file transfer that our runtime can ingest.
[03:29] Maya Chen: compression sounds easiest; is there a perf hit?
[03:32] Samir Patel: minimal for compressible embeddings/prefixes — we saw net improvement at customers with similar tunnels. Also we can batch several small KV ops into one RPC to reduce header overhead.

[03:40] Alex Kim: let's pivot to DNS. Are you using in-VPC resolver endpoints or forwarding to an on-prem resolver?
[03:46] Liam O'Neill: forwards to on-prem resolver, TTLs default to 300s.
[03:50] Samir Patel: forwarding to on-prem means you're touching the VPN for initial name resolution. If the resolver is occasionally slow, initial connections to Redwood endpoints will take longer. Solution: make a local conditional forwarder or use route53 resolver endpoints with cross-account rules. Also set lower TTLs for dynamic endpoints or pin to the PrivateLink endpoint IPs in host maps for the service.
[04:06] Diego Ruiz: there's some config in our automation that re-applies /etc/hosts entries during deploys; that may be clobbering the pins.
[04:12] Jordan Lee: common. We recommend a pinned IP fallback in the app layer for 30s to avoid hitting DNS during critical bursts.

[04:18] [04:20] (brief crosstalk)
[04:23] Samir Patel: On batching — we recommended continuous batching in Redwood runtime, which aggressively coalesces short requests into a stream. But for mixed lengths you want to cap batch token budget and have a separate lane for long sequences. otherwise p99 will suffer.
[04:35] Diego Ruiz: can you give an example config? what's a good token budget and flush timeout?
[04:39] Samir Patel: For your distribution: short bias, try token_budget=1024, max_batch_size=32, short_flush_ms=50, long_lane_threshold=300 tokens. For long lane, use dedicated instances sized for long-seq throughput. We'll send a sample config.
[04:53] Maya Chen: About quantization — we plan to try 8-bit to save cost; worried about hallucinations and quality regression on clinical text.
[04:59] Samir Patel: Important point. int8 quant can shave 30-45% token cost on some kernels, but certain layernorm or softmax-sensitive parts can slip. We recommend: 1) run a small eval suite (100 representative prompts) comparing fp16 vs int8 and measure Rouge/perplexity and a handful of critical medical checks; 2) prefer mixed-precision or per-layer quantization where available.
[05:19] Alex Kim: we can also suggest a rollback policy in Redwood Console — auto-fallback to fp16 if quality regressions exceed threshold during pilot.

[05:27] Liam O'Neill: back to networking, is there anything on the privatelink configuration that might force extra hops?
[05:33] Jordan Lee: Yes: cross-account privatelink endpoints must be in the same AZ ideally, and route tables need specific prefixes. If your caller subnet uses a NAT gateway with a route to 0.0.0.0/0 preferentially, traffic might leave the VPC. Also security groups and NACLs can cause connection resets leading to TCP retries.
[05:48] Diego Ruiz: we did see intermittent connection resets at times that coincide with the p99 spikes.
[05:52] Samir Patel: that can manifest as retransmits and increase observed latency. Also check conntrack table sizes on NAT instances — if exhausted, new flows get delayed.

[06:00] Maya Chen: is there a way to avoid NAT entirely for privatelink lookups?
[06:04] Samir Patel: Yes - ensure the route to the privatelink endpoint is via the VPC endpoint interface (private IP) and that your service discovery resolves to that private IP. Avoid routing through NAT by tightening route table entries for destination prefixes of Redwood endpoints.

[06:12] Alex Kim: let's do a quick live scan of the logs you sent earlier — I have the p99 spike trace open. (Alex shares screen)
[06:20] [06:22] (screen share: p99 spike heatmap)
[06:24] Alex Kim: see these vertical lines — those are times when KV cache miss rates spike and you get bursts of large KV updates. Also note the TCP retransmit markers just before each vertical.
[06:33] Liam O'Neill: yeah that's our daily job runner hitting a heavy generation job.
[06:36] Samir Patel: Make sure heavy offline jobs use a different egress path or a dedicated batch-worker pool so they don't steal connection slots or evict cache entries.

[06:44] Diego Ruiz: question — how does the runtime handle large KV transfer integrity? is there a checksum or windowed ack?
[06:49] Jordan Lee: runtime uses chunked checksums and idempotent apply semantics; if a chunk fails, the runtime will retry only the chunk. But retransmits still cost time.
[06:58] Priya Kapoor: from compliance — we need audit logs for every KV change, who initiated, and retention 1 year. Is that captured?
[07:03] Alex Kim: Yes, Redwood Private can stream audit logs to your S3 or SIEM; we can include KV ops in the audit stream with request IDs. We'll link the log schema.
[07:10] Priya Kapoor: perfect. Please include event schema.

[07:14] Samir Patel: next, quick micro-benchmark plan we recommend you run: 1) MTU ping with increasing payloads to detect fragmentation; 2) KV RPC timing with 1KB, 16KB, 128KB payloads; 3) batching emulation with short/heavy mixes to observe p50/p95/p99; 4) quant eval subset. We'll provide scripts.
[07:32] Maya Chen: can you include expected baseline numbers for our cloud region so we can compare?
[07:36] Samir Patel: yes — we'll include sample p50/p95/p99 numbers for standard privatelink + 10G instance with fp16 and int8 numbers.

[07:44] Alex Kim: Alright let's surface the action items and confirm owners.
[07:48] (quick recap)
[07:50] Alex Kim: Samir to push batching config and quant profiles; Alex to send private link topology doc + security whitepaper; Maya to run tests and share results; follow up call Oct 12.
[07:59] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[08:02] Liam O'Neill: thanks.
[08:03] Alex Kim: Thanks — we'll email notes and scripts.

Questions Raised:
- Can we avoid NAT hairpin without touching on-prem MTU changes?
- How aggressive should batch token budgets be for mixed workloads?
- What is the expected quality delta for int8 on medical prompts?
